raw_response:
I'm fifty this year, been farming this land since I was twenty. Never went to school, can't read the words on the fertilizer bags, but I know my fields. We have six and a half mu — not much, but it's ours. My husband does construction work over in the county town, comes back when the busy seasons hit. My son and daughter-in-law are up in Beijing working, send some money home when they can. At home it's mostly me and my old mother-in-law, though my husband helps out during harvest and planting when he can get away.

I have four mu in wheat-maize, same as always. Two and a half mu on the south side I keep in cotton — that land is a bit sandier and cotton does alright there.

The wheat went in last October, mid-month, right after we got the cotton off that plot. For the base fertilizer I put one big bag of that compound fertilizer per mu — the kind the shop calls "three fifteens," though I don't know what those numbers mean exactly. The neighbor Lao Wang says it's good stuff and his wheat always looks fine, so I do the same. Now it's turning green and I need to topdress. I'll spread about thirty jin of urea per mu when the wheat starts jointing — that's what I've done for years. Wang's wife down the lane uses more, but her husband runs a little shop and they've got more cash than us. I can't afford to throw money around, but I also can't afford a thin crop. I'd rather put a bit too much than too little — a bad year hurts worse than spending a few extra yuan.

For water, I'll irrigate the wheat three times: once now when it's greening up, once at jointing, and once when the grain is filling. The pump electricity isn't cheap, so I watch it, but dry wheat won't give you a damn thing. I flood it like everyone else around here — no fancy sprinklers.

For the cotton, I'll plant in mid-April when the soil warms up. I bought the seed from the supply store, the kind with the pink coating — I don't remember the name but it grew fine last year. I put two cartloads of farmyard manure on that plot, plus about one big bag of compound fertilizer for the whole two and a half mu. If it grows well and sets flowers nicely, I'll topdress maybe half a bag of urea across the plot at flowering time. Cotton needs water when it flowers, so I'll irrigate twice — once at flowering, once when the bolls are filling. Not too much though, or it grows too tall and drops buds. Cotton needs a lot of hand-picking. Me and my husband can handle some, but with him away and my mother-in-law too old to bend down all day, I'll need to hire a few pickers come autumn. They get paid by the catty, so that's money I have to keep in mind.

For summer maize, after we cut the wheat in early June, we have to plant fast — usually three or four days, the window is tight. I hire Lao Zhang's tractor to chop the wheat straw and plant the maize in one go. I buy hybrid seed from the seed shop, about three jin per mu. I put fertilizer down with the planter — about half a bag of compound fertilizer per mu, maybe twenty-five jin. If the rains come good at jointing, that's enough. If it's dry like two years ago, I'll spread some extra urea. Maize doesn't need as much water as wheat — maybe irrigate once or twice if the weather turns dry.

Money is always tight. Last year the wheat price was okay but cotton wasn't great. I have to watch my spending, but wheat is my main food and income crop so I make sure it gets fed. For cotton and maize I can trim back a little if I need to. That's how I always think — don't be stupid with money, but don't starve your crops either.
